punjab.name: Punjab
punjab.tagline: Fertile plains, winter fields and a food culture shaped by farming and hospitality.
punjab.geography: Punjab lies in the north-western Indus plains. The Sutlej, Beas and Ravi, fertile soils and canal irrigation support wheat, mustard, pulses and dairy. Cool winters bring leafy greens to the table; migration and trade have also shaped regional food.
punjab.culinaryLandscape: Punjabi food varies by district and community. Wheat breads, dairy, pulses, mustard greens and tandoor cooking are widely recognised, alongside langar traditions and a strong street-food culture.

dishes.name: Sarson da Saag with Makki di Roti
dishes.descriptor: Winter greens with maize flatbread
dishes.overview: A winter meal of slow-cooked mustard greens with hand-patted maize flatbread. It is often finished with ghee or white butter and served with radish, jaggery or lassi.
steps: Wash and chop the greens. Simmer with ginger, garlic, chillies, salt and a little water until soft.
Mash or blend coarsely. Add a little maize-flour slurry if a thicker saag is preferred.
Temper with ghee, garlic and optional onion; simmer until combined.
Mix maize flour with warm water and salt. Pat into flat rounds by hand.
Cook on a hot griddle, turning carefully. Finish with ghee or butter and serve with the saag.
dishes.history: The pairing grew from seasonal farming and household cooking; no single inventor is documented. Mustard greens are a winter crop. Maize reached India after the Columbian exchange, but its route and timing remain debated. Makki di roti is best understood as part of an evolving Punjabi food tradition, not an unchanged ancient staple.
dishes.imageHint: Look for dated Punjab mustard harvests, winter kitchens or traditional hearths. Caption the date, place, photographer and archive.
dishes.imageQuery: Punjab winter mustard harvest village kitchen sarson saag historical photograph

oralNarrative.role: Home cook from Faisalabad, described by food writer Bisma Tirmizi
oralNarrative.account: In a first-person food essay, Bisma Tirmizi recounts learning the family method from Anjum Khala. Khala says it came from her mother-in-law in Rupnagar, in pre-Partition Punjab, and was passed down through generations. This is a reported family memory, not a surviving old written recipe.
oralNarrative.sourceTitle: Food Stories: Sarson ka Saag / Makki ki Roti

dishes.name: Chole Bhature
dishes.descriptor: Spiced chickpeas with puffed fried bread
dishes.overview: Spiced chickpeas simmered in a thick masala and served with deep-fried, leavened bhature. Pickled onion, chutney and green chilli often accompany it.
ingredients: Coriander, cumin, chilli and garam masala
Maida or wheat flour, yoghurt and leavening
steps: Soak chickpeas overnight and cook until tender.
Cook onion, ginger and garlic. Add tomato and spices to make a thick masala.
Add chickpeas and some cooking liquid; simmer until the gravy thickens.
Make a soft dough with flour, yoghurt, salt and leavening. Rest, then roll into rounds.
Deep-fry until puffed and golden. Serve hot with the chole.
dishes.history: Chickpea curries and fried breads have longer, separate histories across North India; the pairing's exact origin is disputed. A family account from Sita Ram Diwan Chand describes selling chole bhature from a pushcart in Paharganj after Partition. It documents one influential Delhi story, not the dish's sole invention.
dishes.imageHint: Search dated Paharganj street scenes, early chole-bhature stalls or post-Partition Delhi food markets. Treat family recollections as oral history, not proof of sole invention.
dishes.imageQuery: 1950s Paharganj Delhi street food pushcart Sita Ram Diwan Chand chole bhature

sources.title: From Paharganj to Delhi Favourite | Since 1955

sources.note: First-party family account; useful for the business's claimed 1955 founding.

sources.title: Families in Food: Spice Station
sources.note: Reported history and family recollections about the Paharganj shop.

oralNarrative.role: Grandson of Sita Ram, as identified in the NDTV Food report
oralNarrative.account: Pran Nath Kohli recalls his grandfather and Diwan Chand selling chole bhature from a pushcart in Paharganj after Partition, before moving into a shop. This is a family account of one Delhi business, not proof of the dish's sole origin.
oralNarrative.sourceTitle: Sita Ram Diwan Chand: Why Delhi's Heart Is Set on This Chole-Bhature Wala Since 50 Years

west-bengal.name: West Bengal
west-bengal.tagline: A river-and-delta cuisine shaped by rice, fish, mustard and sweets.
west-bengal.geography: West Bengal runs from the Himalayan foothills to the Ganga delta and Bay of Bengal. Rivers, ponds and wetlands support freshwater fish; rice, mustard, vegetables and coastal produce shape everyday cooking.
west-bengal.culinaryLandscape: Bengali food often pairs rice with fish, vegetables and mustard-based preparations. Milk sweets are also important. Recipes differ between the hills, delta, coast and city kitchens.

dishes.name: Shorshe Ilish
dishes.descriptor: Hilsa cooked with mustard and green chilli
dishes.overview: Hilsa is cooked in a pungent mustard paste with green chillies, turmeric and mustard oil. It may be steamed or gently simmered; the sharp sauce balances the fish's rich flavour.
steps: Soak mustard seeds briefly, then grind with green chillies, salt and a little water.
Rub the fish with turmeric and salt.
Warm mustard oil. Add the mustard paste with water and green chillies.
Add the fish and steam or simmer gently until just cooked. Avoid stirring roughly.
dishes.history: Hilsa has long been part of Bengal's river and estuary foodways. Mustard oil is now a defining flavour, but its social status changed over time. Food historian Chitrita Banerji notes that some nineteenth-century elite households in Calcutta did not readily accept it. This shows how regional tastes also evolve.
dishes.imageHint: Look for dated hilsa landings, Hooghly fish markets, river fishing or Bengali household kitchens. Record the collection and date.
dishes.imageQuery: Hilsa fish market Hooghly river Bengal historical photograph

sources.title: The infinite importance of the 'kick' of mustard oil
sources.note: Discusses Chitrita Banerji's account of changing social attitudes to mustard oil.

sources.title: Regional Cuisines of India — II
sources.note: Documents mustard oil and mustard paste as characteristic ingredients in Bengali cooking.

dishes.name: Banglar Rosogolla
dishes.descriptor: Chhana dumplings poached in sugar syrup
dishes.overview: Fresh chhana is kneaded into smooth balls, cooked in boiling sugar syrup and left to soak. The texture depends on the chhana, kneading and syrup.
ingredients: A little semolina or flour in some versions
steps: Curdle hot milk with lemon juice or another food acid; drain the chhana in a clean cloth.
Rinse and press until moist but not watery.
Knead until smooth and roll into crack-free balls.
Boil sugar and water. Add the balls with enough room to expand.
Cook until spongy, then cool in the syrup before serving.
dishes.history: The history of rasgulla is contested between Odisha and Bengal, and the surviving record is incomplete. Bengal's modern commercial story is strongly linked with Nabin Chandra Das in nineteenth-century Calcutta. This entry documents the Bengali tradition without claiming an uncontested single origin.
dishes.imageHint: Search old Kolkata sweet shops, chhana-making workshops or confectioners' kitchens. Verify the date and repository before calling an image historical.
dishes.imageQuery: Kolkata old sweet shop Nabin Chandra Das rosogolla historical photograph

sources.title: Rasgulla — the ethnic Indian sweetmeat delicacy and its evolutionary journey through contemporary research
sources.note: Reviews both Bengal and Odisha traditions and the nineteenth-century Kolkata development account.

tamil-nadu.name: Tamil Nadu
tamil-nadu.tagline: A varied food culture shaped by paddy fields, dry plains, coastal trade and temple towns.
tamil-nadu.geography: Tamil Nadu includes the Coromandel coast, Kaveri delta, dry interior plains and southern uplands. Rice is central in many areas; millets, pulses, coconut, tamarind and spices vary by region.
tamil-nadu.culinaryLandscape: Tamil Nadu has distinct food traditions in Chettinad, Kongunadu, the Kaveri delta, Madurai and the coast. Rice dishes, lentils, fermented foods and festival preparations are common, but recipes vary locally.

dishes.name: Sakkarai Pongal
dishes.descriptor: Sweet rice and lentils for the harvest festival
dishes.overview: Rice and moong dal are cooked until soft, then sweetened with jaggery and finished with ghee, cardamom, cashews and raisins. It is closely associated with Thai Pongal.
steps: Rinse the rice and roast the moong dal lightly.
Cook both with water or milk until very soft.
Dissolve jaggery in a little water and strain.
Stir the syrup into the rice mixture and simmer briefly.
Finish with ghee, cardamom, cashews and raisins.
dishes.history: Thai Pongal is a January harvest festival. Families cook rice as an offering of thanks for the harvest, the Sun and cattle. Sweet pongal is a festive preparation, but the exact origin date of today's recipe is not established by the sources used here.
dishes.imageHint: Look for dated Pongal celebrations, outdoor cooking pots, paddy harvests or family festival photographs. Preserve the original caption and date.
dishes.imageQuery: old Tamil Nadu Pongal harvest festival traditional pot cooking historical photograph

sources.title: Festivals and Events — Pongal (Harvest Festival)
sources.publisher: Madurai District Administration, Government of Tamil Nadu
sources.note: Documents Pongal as a harvest festival honouring the Sun, nature and cattle.

dishes.name: Chicken Chettinad
dishes.descriptor: Chicken in a freshly ground, aromatic spice masala
dishes.overview: Chicken is simmered in a freshly ground masala that often includes pepper, fennel, dried chillies, coconut and local spices. Recipes differ between Chettinad households.
ingredients: Dried red chillies, cinnamon and cloves
Kalpasi or other local spices, where used
steps: Dry-roast the whole spices and coconut; cool and grind.
Sauté curry leaves, onion, ginger and garlic in oil.
Add tomato and the ground masala. Cook until aromatic.
Add chicken, salt and a little water. Cover and cook until tender.
Reduce the gravy to the preferred consistency and finish with curry leaves.
dishes.history: Chettinad is associated with the Nattukottai Chettiar community of Tamil Nadu. Its trading networks and travel helped shape a cuisine known for layered spice blends. Chicken Chettinad is a regional style, not one fixed recipe with a known inventor.
dishes.imageHint: Search archival Chettinad home photographs, spice preparation, traditional kitchens or old Chettinad houses. Keep modern dish photos labelled as contemporary.
dishes.imageQuery: Chettinad Karaikudi old merchant house kitchen spice trade archival photograph

sources.title: Chettinad, Village Clusters of the Tamil Merchants

sources.note: Documents the Chettinad region and Nattukottai Chettiar merchant networks.

sources.title: Chettinad Cuisine
sources.note: Describes characteristic spices and cooking traditions.

kerala.name: Kerala
kerala.tagline: A coastal and backwater cuisine built around rice, coconut, spices and shared meals.
kerala.geography: Kerala lies between the Arabian Sea and Western Ghats. Monsoon rainfall, backwaters, paddy fields and spice-growing hills support rice, coconut, plantain, pepper, ginger and a wide range of fish and vegetables.
kerala.culinaryLandscape: Kerala food includes banana-leaf feasts, rice breakfasts, coconut-rich curries and coastal fish dishes. Malabar, central Kerala and Travancore have distinct traditions.

dishes.name: Kerala Sadya
dishes.descriptor: A ceremonial vegetarian feast served on a banana leaf
dishes.overview: Sadya is a ceremonial vegetarian feast served on a banana leaf. Rice is accompanied by curries, vegetable dishes, pickles, savouries and payasam; the exact menu varies.
ingredients: Curry leaves, mustard seeds and chillies
steps: Prepare the dishes separately: dal, sambar, avial, thoran, olan, pachadi and pickles are common examples.
Cook the rice and place a clean banana leaf before the guest.
Arrange the accompaniments in the customary order; local practice varies.
Serve rice with the curries and side dishes.
Finish with payasam and the customary savouries.
dishes.history: Sadya is a form of festive hospitality in Kerala, not a single recipe. Onam sadya is its best-known form, but similar feasts are served at weddings and other celebrations. Kerala Tourism documents the leaf arrangement, serving customs and regional variations.
dishes.imageHint: Look for dated Onam feasts, wedding sadya service or community banana-leaf meals. Identify the event, location, date and photographer.
dishes.imageQuery: Kerala historical Onam sadya banana leaf feast archival photograph

sources.title: Sadya — the traditional vegetarian feast of Keralites
sources.note: Official description of leaf arrangement, component dishes and serving sequence.

sources.title: Onasadhya — A Feast of Delicacies
sources.note: Explains the association between sadya and Onam.

dishes.name: Puttu and Kadala Curry
dishes.descriptor: Steamed rice cylinders with black-chickpea curry
dishes.overview: Puttu is steamed rice flour layered with grated coconut. It is commonly served with kadala curry, a spiced black-chickpea preparation.
ingredients: Onion or shallots, ginger and garlic
Coconut oil, mustard seeds and curry leaves
steps: Soak black chickpeas overnight and cook until tender.
Roast coconut, shallots, chilli and coriander; grind to a paste.
Temper mustard seeds and curry leaves. Add onion, chickpeas and the paste; simmer.
Moisten rice flour with salted water until crumbly, not dough-like.
Layer rice flour and coconut in a puttu steamer; steam until cooked.
dishes.history: Puttu and kadala curry are a familiar breakfast pairing in Kerala. The dish uses rice flour and coconut, while the curry uses black chickpeas. Kerala Tourism documents the preparation, but does not establish a single inventor or exact origin date.
dishes.imageHint: Search dated Kerala kitchen photographs, traditional puttu steamers or household breakfast scenes. Do not label a modern utensil as antique.
dishes.imageQuery: traditional Kerala puttu kudam steamer black chickpea curry archival kitchen

sources.title: Puttu and Kadala Curry
sources.note: Official ingredient list and method for puttu and kadala curry.

sources.title: Nadan Food — Ethnic Cuisine
sources.note: Documents puttu and kadala curry in local food experiences.

rajasthan.name: Rajasthan
rajasthan.tagline: A cuisine shaped by arid landscapes, durable ingredients and hospitality.
rajasthan.geography: Rajasthan includes the Thar Desert, Aravalli range and semi-arid plains. Water scarcity and seasonal produce encouraged the use of pulses, gram flour, millet, wheat, dairy and preserved foods.
rajasthan.culinaryLandscape: Rajasthani food is more than royal cuisine. Everyday meals use breads, pulses, dairy, gram flour and preserved vegetables. Dishes differ between desert districts, eastern plains and Mewar.

dishes.name: Dal Baati Churma
dishes.descriptor: Baked wheat rolls, lentils and sweetened crushed bread
dishes.overview: Baati (firm wheat rolls) is served with lentil dal and churma, a sweet made from crushed wheat and ghee. It is a well-known Rajasthani meal served at family gatherings and feasts.
steps: Make a firm wheat dough with ghee, salt and water; shape into balls.
Bake or roast the baati until browned and cooked through.
Cook the lentils until soft; temper with ghee and spices.
Crush some baati and mix with jaggery or sugar and ghee for churma.
Serve baati with dal, churma and chutney.
dishes.history: Dal baati churma is strongly associated with Rajasthan. A popular legend links baati to Mewar ruler Bappa Rawal, but clear evidence for that specific story is limited. The better-supported context is practical: wheat, pulses and ghee suit local food economies and can be cooked with simple equipment and fuel.
dishes.imageHint: Look for archival Mewar kitchens, clay ovens, traditional baati roasting or dated feast photographs. Do not illustrate the Bappa Rawal legend as fact.
dishes.imageQuery: Rajasthan traditional baati clay oven old village cooking photograph

sources.note: Official description of the three components and serving style.

sources.title: Cuisine of Rajasthan

dishes.name: Gatte ki Sabzi
dishes.descriptor: Gram-flour dumplings in a spiced yoghurt gravy
dishes.overview: Seasoned gram-flour dough is shaped into logs, boiled and sliced. The pieces are simmered in a tangy yoghurt gravy.
steps: Mix besan with salt, spices, carom seeds and a little oil; add water to form a firm dough.
Roll into logs and simmer in salted water until cooked.
Cool and slice the logs into discs.
Whisk yoghurt with spices and a little water.
Temper cumin and asafoetida, add the yoghurt mixture and gatte, then simmer gently.
dishes.history: Rajasthan Foundation notes that arid conditions and limited fresh vegetables helped make gram flour, grains and dairy important in the state's food. Gatte uses stored besan to make a filling dish. The available sources do not establish a single origin story or inventor.
dishes.imageHint: Look for dated Rajasthan kitchen photographs, besan grinding, earthen cooking vessels or regional food documentation. Label modern dish photos accurately.

gujarat.name: Gujarat
gujarat.tagline: A cuisine of seasonal vegetables, grains, pulses and fermented foods.
gujarat.geography: Gujarat spans the Rann of Kutch, Kathiawar, river plains and the coast. Its dry and fertile zones support different crops, including millets, pulses, vegetables and dairy produce.
gujarat.culinaryLandscape: Gujarati food includes farsan, fermented batters, vegetable dishes, breads and seasonal one-pot meals. Vegetarian traditions are strong in many communities, while coastal foodways also include fish.

dishes.name: Undhiyu
dishes.descriptor: Winter vegetables slow-cooked in an inverted clay pot
dishes.overview: Undhiyu combines winter vegetables, beans, stuffed aubergines and methi muthia. Traditionally, the ingredients are layered in a clay pot and slow-cooked.
steps: Grind green garlic, coriander, coconut, sesame, spices and lemon into a coarse masala.
Stuff the aubergines and cut the other vegetables.
Make methi muthia with fenugreek leaves, gram flour and spices.
Layer vegetables and muthia in a heavy pot with masala and a little water.
Cover and cook slowly until tender; turn gently.
dishes.history: Undhiyu is associated with the winter harvest of south Gujarat, especially Surat. Gujarat Tourism describes cooking vegetables in a clay pot called a matla, placed upside down over heat. The name is linked to undhu, Gujarati for 'upside down'.
dishes.imageHint: Search dated Surat winter markets, matla cooking, outdoor village fires or community undhiyu gatherings.
dishes.imageQuery: Surat Gujarat undhiyu matla earthen pot upside down cooking historical image

sources.title: Undhiyu

sources.title: Winter brings undhiyu parties to the yard

dishes.name: Dhokla
dishes.descriptor: A soft, savoury steamed batter preparation
dishes.overview: Dhokla is a savoury steamed cake made from fermented rice-and-pulse batter or, in popular versions, gram flour. It is cut into pieces and finished with a mustard-seed and curry-leaf tempering.
ingredients: Rice and chana dal, or gram flour depending on style
Natural fermentation or fruit salt for quick versions
steps: For a fermented version, soak rice and chana dal, grind and leave until aerated.
Season with salt, ginger and chilli. Add fruit salt only for a quick version.
Pour into a greased pan and steam until set.
Cool slightly and cut into squares.
Temper mustard seeds, curry leaves and chillies in oil; pour over the dhokla.
dishes.history: A 2022 review in the Journal of Applied Microbiology notes a reference to a possible precursor called dukkia in Gujarati Jain literature dated to 1066 CE. This is not proof that today's dhokla recipe existed unchanged then. Khaman, made mainly from gram flour, is related but distinct.
dishes.imageHint: Look for catalogued Gujarati Jain manuscripts mentioning dukkia, early farsan shops or traditional steaming vessels. Cite the repository and folio for manuscripts.

maharashtra.name: Maharashtra
maharashtra.tagline: From Deccan grain kitchens to Mumbai street stalls, food reflects regional life and migration.
maharashtra.geography: Maharashtra stretches from the Konkan coast across the Western Ghats to the Deccan plateau and Vidarbha. Coastal cooking uses rice, coconut and fish; the interior uses jowar, bajra, pulses and groundnuts.
maharashtra.culinaryLandscape: Konkan, Desh, Vidarbha, Khandesh and Mumbai have distinct food traditions. Bhakri meals, lentil dishes, festival sweets and city snacks form part of this varied cuisine.

dishes.name: Vada Pav
dishes.descriptor: Spiced potato fritter served in a soft bread roll
dishes.overview: A spiced potato fritter is coated in gram-flour batter, deep-fried and served inside a pav roll. Garlic chutney, green chutney and fried chilli are common accompaniments.
ingredients: Mustard seeds, turmeric and curry leaves
Dry garlic chutney and green chutney
steps: Boil and mash potatoes. Mix with a tempering of mustard seeds, curry leaves, turmeric, chilli, ginger and garlic.
Shape the potato mixture into balls.
Make a thick gram-flour batter with salt and turmeric.
Dip the balls in batter and deep-fry until crisp.
Serve inside pav with chutneys and fried chilli.
dishes.history: Vada pav is a modern Mumbai street food. A 2015 Cultural Anthropology study traces its parts to different food histories: pav to Portuguese-influenced and migrant bakery culture, and vada to regional snack traditions. The story that vendor Ashok Vaidya paired them in the 1960s is widely reported, but not proven as the only origin.
dishes.imageHint: Search dated 1960s–1980s Mumbai street stalls, Dadar vendors, mill-worker food scenes or early vada-pav carts. Treat the Ashok Vaidya story as a reported origin.
dishes.imageQuery: Mumbai 1960s street vendor vada pav Dadar textile mill historical photograph

dishes.name: Puran Poli
dishes.descriptor: Sweet lentil-and-jaggery flatbread
dishes.overview: A thin flatbread is filled with cooked chana dal and jaggery, flavoured with cardamom or nutmeg. It is griddled and usually served with ghee.
steps: Cook chana dal until tender; drain well.
Cook the dal with jaggery until thick, then mash until smooth.
Add cardamom and nutmeg; cool the filling.
Knead a soft flour dough and let it rest.
Wrap the filling in dough, roll gently and cook on a hot griddle with ghee.
dishes.history: Puran poli is a festive sweet in Maharashtra, including at Gudi Padwa. A food-technology review cites a related preparation called purana in the twelfth-century text Manasollasa. This is an antecedent reference, not proof that today's recipe was identical.
dishes.imageHint: Look for dated Gudi Padwa meals, family festival cooking, traditional puran presses or old Pune household kitchens.

karnataka.name: Karnataka
karnataka.tagline: A varied food culture, from coastal rice dishes to the millet traditions of the Deccan.
karnataka.geography: Karnataka spans the Konkan and Malnad, the Kaveri basin, the dry Deccan plateau and northern districts. Rice, ragi, jowar, pulses, coconut and tamarind are used differently across these regions.
karnataka.culinaryLandscape: Coastal, Udupi, Kodava, North Karnataka and Mysuru-Bengaluru cuisines are distinct. Everyday millet meals, tiffin dishes, temple foodways and festival sweets all have a place.

dishes.name: Mysore Pak
dishes.descriptor: A ghee-rich sweet of gram flour and sugar
dishes.overview: Mysore Pak is made by cooking gram flour with ghee and sugar syrup until it sets. It may be soft and porous or firmer and crumbly.
steps: Sieve gram flour and roast lightly in some ghee.
Prepare a sugar syrup.
Add the flour gradually, stirring to prevent lumps.
Add hot ghee in batches and stir until the mixture thickens.
Pour into a greased tray, set and cut while slightly warm.
dishes.history: Mysore Pak is linked by local tradition to the Mysore Palace kitchen during the Wadiyar period. The popular story names palace cook Kakasura Madappa. A descendant's account preserves this family memory, but it is not a surviving palace recipe record.
dishes.imageHint: Search dated Mysore Palace food-service photographs, old Mysuru sweet shops or early Guru Sweets images. Keep family photographs distinct from palace records.
dishes.imageQuery: Mysore Palace kitchen Kakasura Madappa Mysore Pak old sweet shop historical photograph

oralNarrative.account: In a 2019 interview, Shivanand Madappa recounts the family story that his great-grandfather Kakasura Madappa prepared the sweet for the Mysore kings. The article calls this an apocryphal family tradition, not a verified palace record.

dishes.name: Bisi Bele Bath
dishes.descriptor: Hot rice, lentils, vegetables and tamarind
dishes.overview: A hot rice-and-lentil dish cooked with vegetables, tamarind and a roasted spice blend. It is often finished with ghee, cashews and curry leaves.
ingredients: Carrot, beans, peas or other vegetables
Chana dal, urad dal and dry coconut for masala
steps: Cook rice and toor dal until soft; cook the vegetables until tender.
Roast and grind the spices with lentils and dry coconut.
Prepare tamarind extract and add it to the vegetables.
Combine rice, dal, vegetables, tamarind and spice powder; simmer until thick.
Finish with a ghee tempering of cashews and curry leaves.
dishes.history: Bisi bele bath is associated with the Mysuru-Bengaluru region. Its name means 'hot lentil-rice'. Tourism sources document its ingredients and popularity, but do not establish a reliable inventor or exact origin date; a palace-invention story is therefore not used here.
dishes.imageHint: Look for old Mysuru or Bengaluru household cookbooks, brass cooking vessels, early eateries or dated family meal photographs.
dishes.imageQuery: Karnataka old cookbook bisi bele bath Mysore traditional kitchen archival photograph

sources.title: Bisi Bele Bath
sources.note: Lists the core ingredients and preparation method.

uttar-pradesh.name: Uttar Pradesh
uttar-pradesh.tagline: A broad food landscape shaped by the Ganga plains, pilgrimage towns and Awadh's kitchens.
uttar-pradesh.geography: Uttar Pradesh spans the Ganga-Yamuna Doab, eastern plains, Terai foothills and historic Awadh. Wheat, rice, pulses, dairy and seasonal vegetables shape everyday meals; river fish is important in some areas.
uttar-pradesh.culinaryLandscape: The state includes Awadhi slow-cooked dishes, Banarasi street food, western UP breads and dairy, and eastern UP rice and lentils. Lucknow's kebabs are one regional tradition, not the whole state's cuisine.

dishes.name: Galouti Kebab
dishes.descriptor: Fine-textured minced meat kebab from Lucknow
dishes.overview: Finely minced meat is mixed with raw papaya, aromatics and spices, shaped into small patties and shallow-fried in ghee. It is often served with paratha or roomali roti.
steps: Grind the meat until very fine.
Mix with papaya, ginger-garlic, fried onion and spices.
Rest briefly so the papaya can tenderise the meat.
Shape into small, flat patties.
Cook gently in ghee until set and lightly browned.
dishes.history: Galouti kebab belongs to Lucknow's Awadhi kebab tradition. A popular story links its soft texture to Nawab Asaf-ud-Daula's difficulty chewing, but this is a culinary legend, not a dated kitchen record. The wider context is the refinement of minced-meat kebabs in Awadh.

dishes.name: Awadhi Dum Pukht Biryani
dishes.descriptor: Rice and meat slowly cooked in a sealed vessel
dishes.overview: Marinated meat and partly cooked rice are layered in a heavy vessel, sealed with dough and cooked slowly. The trapped steam finishes the rice and meat together.
steps: Marinate the meat with yoghurt, ginger-garlic, fried onion and spices.
Parboil the rice with whole spices; drain while still firm.
Layer meat and rice in a heavy handi with herbs and ghee.
Seal the lid with dough to keep steam inside.
Cook over low heat until the meat and rice are done; rest before opening.
dishes.history: Dum pukht means slow cooking in a sealed vessel and is closely associated with Lucknow's Awadhi food culture. Popular stories about its origin are difficult to verify. This entry focuses on the documented cooking method and its regional association, not a single inventor.

assam.name: Assam
assam.tagline: A riverine cuisine of rice, freshwater fish, sour broths and banana-ash preparations.
assam.geography: Assam is shaped by the Brahmaputra and Barak valleys, wetlands, floodplains and heavy monsoon rainfall. Rice, freshwater fish, banana plants, bamboo shoots and souring fruits are important in many local foodways.
assam.culinaryLandscape: Assamese meals may include khar, an alkaline preparation, and tenga, a light sour curry, with rice, greens and fish. Ingredients and recipes vary across the state's communities.

dishes.name: Assamese Khar
dishes.descriptor: An alkaline preparation made with plant-ash filtrate
dishes.overview: Khar is both an alkaline cooking ingredient and dishes made with it. Kola khar is filtered from banana-plant ash and used in preparations with papaya, pulses or vegetables.
steps: Prepare kola khar using a documented food-safe household method for banana-plant ash.
After the ash cools, pass water through it and filter the liquid. Never use unknown or treated ash.
Cook papaya, pulses or vegetables until nearly tender.
Add a measured amount of khar filtrate and simmer briefly.
Serve with rice. Ingredients and methods vary by household.
dishes.history: Khar is an Assamese food technique, not just a seasoning. A 2020 Journal of Ethnic Foods study documents banana trunk, rhizome and peels being dried, burned and filtered with water to make kolakhar. The method reflects local plant knowledge and household practice.
dishes.imageHint: Look for ethnographic photographs of banana-ash preparation, bamboo sieves or Assamese kitchens. Record community, place, date and photographer.

dishes.name: Masor Tenga
dishes.descriptor: Light, sour fish curry with seasonal ingredients
dishes.overview: A light fish curry with a gentle sourness. Tomato, lemon, thekera, elephant apple, roselle or raw mango may be used, depending on season and household.
steps: Clean the fish and rub with turmeric and salt.
Lightly fry the pieces in mustard oil; set aside.
Temper whole spices and add tomato or another souring ingredient.
Add water and simmer to make a light broth.
Return the fish and simmer gently until cooked; finish with chilli and herbs.
dishes.history: Masor tenga is a familiar sour fish preparation in Assam. Assam Tourism lists several local souring ingredients, showing that tenga is a flexible method shaped by season and produce rather than one fixed recipe with a known inventor.
